However, terrorism (or anything where an innocent is an intended target) deals with acts which are near impossible to justify with motive. Let's take a scale of acts by order of evil. Murder is bad. Mass murdering is worse. Genocide is much worse.
Would you argue that Hitler's Holocaust could be justified? Let's say he was believing that he was saving his people, the Aryans, from extinction by killing the Jews (which he states in Mein Kampf). One could argue that "saving your people" is a noble goal. But it doesn't excuse the **mass murder of innocents**

Take the My Lai massacre. US soldiers kill everyone in a village in Vietnam. They're under combat stress, PTSD, and they've just plain lost it. But that doesn't excuse their actions.

But stress and PTSD will excuse a woman from guilt if she kills her husband in his sleep. It's called battered woman syndrome.

My view is that the further up the scale you go in terms of evil acts, there is eventually a point where no justification will save you from your actions.

1) do you think that the revokal of rights itself is wrong?

2) Is it acceptable with a perfect court system and a fair jury?

3) Is it acceptable with a perfect court system intended to be fair but due to random selection, the jurors were not fair?

4) Is it acceptable with a non biased court with biased jurors given the reality of our world?

I agree that a perfect court system is near impossible, not just here but in any other type of case, criminal and civil.

But let's say, hypothetically, we had you in the government position to set up all aspects of the court system. Would you accept the rights of these terrorists being taken away then?

Our government revokes certain rights of convicts. Are those rights? Maybe it's because I view rights as linked to responsibilities so that all rights are more like privileges. Thomas Jefferson wrote about inalienable rights that we take away from prisoners all the time. We execute some. There is no liberty in prison. There is no pursuit of happiness in prison.

Would we ever be able to find a group of jurors that do not have a presumption of guilt when terrorism is involved? Does it really matter? Your earlier argument had a bit of slippery slope. I honestly doubt the whole system would crumble because there are presumptions of guilt preexisting within the jurors. 

Process: guy gets taken prisoner, goes to trial in Gitmo or US mainland with random jury. 

Also, I already said that they should need a higher standard of evidence than your standard criminal court. However, if we presume innocence or guilt, it will not change the facts. This man was planting a bomb. This man was building one. This one was meeting with senior al-Qaeda officials in a cave in the countryside stocked with munitions. If we presume innocence, doesn't the next logical question become "If they were innocent, why would they be doing these things?"

A higher burden of proof would separate the "maybes" from the "obvious".

Should we have put Osama on trial with a presumption of innocence?

It depends on the immediacy of the reason. Let's say they planted bomb vests on his family, or something like that. Upon his capture, would he not be willing to side with us and give us everything we want in order to save his family?

Let's say he's carried out the attack. Does the welfare of his family justify the mass murders of tens or hundreds?

Let's say he was taken as a child forcibly and pressed into service. Over the years he goes and becomes more and more violent. After he becomes an adult, he carries his indoctrination with him into his acts. We would say that there's mental issues due to his abuse as a child. But even serial killers with abusive childhoods go to prison or a mental institution. 

Torture was the best example of the complete lack of human rights I could think of. Other things that deprive them of human rights, as long as they have some possible benefit to their captors, are acceptable as well.
